title: Power Forearms: Health for Life (1984)
author: Mithosphere
desc:
We will be working to increase strength, mass, and definition of the major muscle groups in your forearms, wrist flexors/extensors, forearm supinator/pronator, finger flexors/extensors, plus the brachioradialis. Remember, developing balanced strength around the wrist joint greatly reduces your chances of wrist injury during other athletic pursuits.

Our program will incorporate the Fatigue/Tension principle. This means:
- Short rests between exercises for the same muscle group, or no rest between exercises for different muscle groups.
- Use of relatively light weights. General guideline - in a 6 to 8 rep set, the last 2 reps should be nearly impossible.
- Adjusting exercises to match resistance to muscle leverage.

We will let the Interdependency of Muscle Groups dictate exercise order. The result:
- wrist extensor exercises will precede brachioradialis exercises.
- finger flexor exercises will come last.

We will only use exercises that put minimal stress on the elbow and wrist joints.

Should not be done more than three times per week. We recommend two. If possible, arrange your overall workout so there is at least one day after Power Forearms! before working any major upper body muscle group (chest, back, or arms). Performing forearm work one day or less before working chest, back, or arms can result in overstressed wrists, due to the combination of forearm fatigue plus the heavy weights involved in working the upper body. The best time to do Power Forearms! is immediately after you work chest, back, and arms. That way, you allow your forearms maximum recovery time before your next upper body workout.

The same principle applies for martial artists and other athletes. Performing forearm work one day or less before punching the heavy bag increases your risk of wrist injury. Doing Power Forearms! immediately after a heavy bag workout allows your forearms maximum recovery time. Finish your workouts with forearm work.

In this program, you don't rest between supersets. YOU NEVER REST AT ALL! When you finish one exercise, drop the weight, pick up the next one, and keep going. Good Luck!

ss.note: Extend your arms out to your sides. Your hands should be about 18" from your body. Gripping the bars AS TIGHT AS POSSIBLE, twist bars back and forth at a rate of about 1 back/forth twist per second.
Bend arms at elbows so forearms are parallel to the ground, and, once again, twist bars for 45 seconds to a minute.
Grip a barbell, palms up, with your hands about six inches apart. Let the elbows rise up off the bench at the bottom of the motion.
Take a slightly wider than shoulder width grip on a barbell, palms down, and place your forearms on your knees as you sit on an exercise bench.
With your forearms against the outsides of your thighs, grip narrow, and the bar hanging behind you Gripping the bar tightly, curl it up as far as you can. Hold for one second, then lower the bar.
Shoulder-width grip. Your elbows should come slightly forward as you lift, but they should NOT move out sideways!
Reps per side. Stand upright, hold SED as close to unweighted end as possible. Bending only at the wrist, curl the bar up in front of you (like a hammer curl for the wrist).
Reps per side. Stand upright, hold SED as close to unweighted end as possible. Bending only at the wrist, curl the bar up behind you.

ex.note: Reps per hand. Seated, brace your forearm on a bench. Rotate your wrist first to the inside, then to the outside under control, this is one rep.

ss.note: Instead of keeping a tight grip and curling at the wrists, loosen your grip, allow the bar to roll to the tips of your fingers, and then curl it back up at the fingers.
Instead of keeping a tight grip and curling at the wrists, loosen your grip, allow the bar to roll to the tips of your fingers, and then curl it back up at the fingers.

ex.note: Reps per side. Cup your hand over the back of your other hand. You should have contact along the entire length of your fingers. With MODERATE RESISTANCE, straighten the fingers. Not an isometric.
